CONSTITUTIVE INSTRUMENT: a charter, letters patent or act, in the form Harris quotes verbatim at printed 98 - 'one body politic and corporate . . . shall have perpetual succession, and shall have a common seal, and by the name shall and may sue and be sued, and also shall and may have power and authority to purchase lands . . . without incurring any of the penalties or forfeitures of the Statute of Mortmain' (preambles to 6 Geo. III c.96 and c.97, 1766). OUT OF SCOPE, ALL FOUR EXCLUSIONS MAINTAINER-SET. (1) deed_of_settlement_company, the unincorporated counterpart, already coded from Televantos 2020 and not reasoned about here. (2) The VOC and every Dutch company: coded from nowhere in this batch, and in the event Harris 2000 barely mentions them - 'VOC' 2 hits and 'Dutch East India' 2 hits across 349 PDF pages, measured. (3) The pre-1600 regulated, guild, municipal and ecclesiastical corporation. (4) Harris's REGULATED corporation, which is a chartered business corporation but is separated from this row on CI1 and LR3: its members 'traded in their own stock, taking risks and liabilities individually' while the joint-stock corporation 'traded in only one account' (printed 32-33). That exclusion is the coder's, made on the source's own distinction, and is flagged for the maintainer. THE SCOPE RULE THE joint_stock ROW IMPOSES WAS APPLIED CELL BY CELL AND THE JUDGEMENT IS RECORDED IN EACH NOTE: where a source uses 'joint stock company' of an English concern between 1720 and 1844 it may name the unincorporated form, so no cell took a value until the passage was shown to bear on a chartered entity. The one place this mattered is CI2, where Harris's sentence at printed 191 says 'the joint-stock company' and the following page fixes the comparison set as 'the joint-stock corporation, the common-law partnership, and the unincorporated company' (192). SOURCE. Harris, R., Industrializing English Law: Entrepreneurship and Business Organization, 1720-1844 (Cambridge University Press). CITED THROUGHOUT AS Harris 2000. The file's copyright page reads 'Cambridge University Press 2004' over 'First published in printed format 2000' and carries both an eBook and a hardback ISBN (0-511-03380-X, 0-521-66275-3): this is the electronic reissue of the 2000 typesetting, so the pagination is the one the literature cites and the 2000 date is correct. The question was whether the row starts in 1600 with the EIC or in 1720 with the Bubble Act. NEITHER DATE IS A CHANGE POINT IN THE FORM ON HARRIS'S OWN ACCOUNT. Against 1600: the first English corporation to trade on a joint stock was the Russia Company, 'founded in 1553 and chartered in 1555' (printed 43), 'The notion of joint stock only appeared in 1553' (24), and the East India Company, 'initiated in 1599 and chartered in 1600' (43), is not the origin of the form but the one company in which permanent joint stock survived - 'permanent joint-stock turned out to be a problematic and undesirable feature for the early business corporations. It survived only in the exceptional case of the East India Company' (45). A 1600 start therefore rests on a company that is exceptional in Harris's account rather than typical of it. Against 1720: Harris devotes a section to the question and answers it in the negative - the Bubble Act's wording was 'very broad and general', its enforcement weak, and it was 'practically a dead letter' with a single reported eighteenth-century prosecution; 'The Bubble Act was not as well defined a turning point as many have argued and its impact on the developments up to the end of the eighteenth century was minimal' (78-81). THE TITLE'S DATE IS THE BOOK'S PERIODISATION, NOT A CLAIM ABOUT THE INSTITUTION, and it was not inherited. THE PROPOSAL IS 1720-1844 NEVERTHELESS, AND THE REASON IS THE CELLS RATHER THAN THE NARRATIVE. Four coded characteristics take a DIFFERENT value before roughly 1680, so any earlier start would put this row inside the condition that split voc on 2026-08-29 and stripped joint_stock of its cells on 2026-09-06 - a type spanning both values of a characteristic. CI1: several-accounts before the 1620s, the Russia Company reorganised in 1586 on 'several separate accounts, each for a period of one to three years' and moving to 'individual accounts' by 1622-1623 (45); common thereafter (33). CI2: no permanent stock before the 1680s (45), permanent stock in the corporations formed after the Restoration (52). FP2: monopoly 'an almost inherent characteristic of the early business corporations' (41), 'no longer an essential part of every incorporation' after the 1680s (52). MG3: 'The typical charter of a business corporation limited its membership by demanding relatively high membership fees' (41), against open public subscription after 1720 (114). 1844 is the terminal date on the source's own account, the Joint Stock Companies Registration Act being where registration replaces authorisation (282-288). PERIOD AND EVIDENCE ARE NOT CO-EXTENSIVE, AND THIS ROW SAYS SO IN THE HEADER BECAUSE IT IS THIS CENSUS'S STANDING WEAKNESS OF THIS KIND. The claimed period is 1720-1844. THE CODED CELLS REST ON EVIDENCE SPANNING c.1660-1837 AND ARE DENSEST FOR 1766-1825. Four cells - LP1, LP2, LP3 and TS1 - rest on statements of the general law of corporations that Harris dates from the sixteenth century (18-19) together with acts of 1733 and 1766 (94, 98), so they are stable across and beyond the claimed period. CI3, CI4 and MG3 rest on 1740-1825 evidence (114, 117-118). FP4 rests partly on 1786-1837 statutes (274-277) and would flip to 1 at 1844 by definition. NOT ONE CELL RESTS ON EVIDENCE FROM 1720-1740, the first two decades the row claims. A REVIEWER SHOULD READ THIS ROW AS A ROW ABOUT c.1740-1830 THAT CLAIMS 1720-1844. name: Deed of settlement company (English unincorporated joint-stock company)
period: c.1720-1844 (Bubble Act 1720 to the Joint Stock Companies Act 1844); ALL CODED CELLS REST ON 1790-1827 EVIDENCE

SCOPE, WRITTEN 2026-09-05 BECAUSE THE WORKING SLUG NAMED A CLASS AND THE ROW MUST FIX ITS OWN REFERENT: the English UNINCORPORATED JOINT-STOCK COMPANY constituted by DEED OF SETTLEMENT - a partnership whose elaborately drafted articles excluded the default partnership rules and settled legal title to the circulating trade assets on a fixed body of trustees, with control divided between directors, a general court of proprietors and those trustees. CONSTITUTIVE INSTRUMENT: the deed of settlement (the articles of association), a private deed, with no Royal Charter, patent or Act of Parliament. Televantos's own glossary treats 'deed of settlement company' and 'joint stock company' as one term: 'A business which raised capital by issuing shares and/or bonds. This was distinct from a typical partnership, where the partners who managed the business provided the capital. Legally, deed of settlement companies were partnerships, but made use of some rules of trusts law in an attempt to emulate the benefits of incorporation' (printed 183).
THE UNIT IS THE DEED-OF-SETTLEMENT COMPANY AND NOT THE WIDER CLASS OF ENGLISH ASSOCIATIONS CONSTITUTED BY TRUST DEED, AND THE REASON IS EVIDENTIAL RATHER THAN TIDY. Televantos's chapter 2 treats TWO trust-using business forms, and they take OPPOSITE VALUES on the census's owner-shielding question. The deed-of-settlement company had none: its shareholders were partners, personally liable without limit, and clauses purporting to limit that liability 'were not fully effective' (44-46, 172). The TESTAMENTARY TRADING TRUST did: on Ex p Garland (1804) the trustee's indemnity, and so the trade creditors' reach into the testamentary estate, was capped at the sum the will set aside, which Televantos calls in terms 'an example of how trusts could create limited liability trading entities' (56-60). A single row spanning both would take both values on AP3 and LR1, which is the condition under which voc was split on 2026-08-29 and under which partenrederij was held apart from the open rederij on 2026-08-29. The testamentary trading trust is in any case not an association - it has no members - and is proposed as an ACQUISITION, not as a row.
ALSO OUT OF SCOPE: the ordinary Regency partnership of owner-managers (Televantos chapter 1), whose default rules this form's deed exists to displace; jointly run shipping and mining businesses, which 'were not treated as partnerships' (16 n 5); and chartered or statutory corporations, whose privileges 'lay in the gift of the Crown or Parliament' (172).
BOUNDARY WITH THE EXISTING joint_stock ROW, RESOLVED ON THE EVIDENCE AND FLAGGED FOR DOCUMENTATION. joint_stock reads 'Joint-stock corporation | European | 17c onward | Harris 2020' and carries NO SCOPE NOTE, and Televantos's glossary makes 'joint stock company' a synonym for the present form. But joint_stock is NOT uncoded - it carries two cells, and its LP1=1 has the cell note 'chartered legal personhood', which fixes its referent as the CHARTERED corporation. This row codes LP1=0. The two therefore differ on the first characteristic either touches and there is no coding collision. A draft scope note for joint_stock, to be applied with this batch rather than ahead of it, is at proposed-of/PATCH-joint-stock-scope-2026-09-05.md; it also flags that joint_stock is on its face an umbrella over the three coded voc rows.
PERIOD AND EVIDENCE ARE NOT CO-EXTENSIVE, AND THAT IS THIS ROW'S MAIN WEAKNESS - the partenrederij problem again. The period claimed runs from the Bubble Act 1720, which by making it an offence to raise capital by issuing transferable stock without Charter or Act drove counsel to invent the form (35-36), to the Joint Stock Companies Act 1844, which forced large partnerships to incorporate by registration (52). EVERY CODED CELL RESTS ON EVIDENCE FROM 1790-1827, the period Televantos's book covers, supplemented by his reading of DuBois (1938) for the eighteenth century and of Freeman, Pearson and Taylor (2012), who find that 209 of the 224 large partnerships they examine between 1720 and 1840 used trusts in their articles (31). FP4 in particular would flip at 1844 by definition.
